subtype: Patterns triggered by a partner's style [Observer]
passage: I'm Madhuri's younger brother, and I've shared a flat with her and Jeevan since June. I've watched the same loop maybe ten times. Something small goes wrong, like Jeevan forgetting to call from a work trip. Madhuri asks what's wrong, then asks again, louder. Jeevan says "Nothing," and goes to the balcony. She follows. He puts his earphones in. She cries; he goes for a drive. Last Sunday something changed. Madhuri drew two arrows on the fridge whiteboard, one chasing, one running, making a circle. "This is us," she said. "Not you, not me. Us." Jeevan actually laughed. Then he stayed at the table. I don't know what they were feeling inside, but they talked for an hour.

qa.q: What did Madhuri draw on the fridge whiteboard?
qa.a: She drew two arrows, one chasing and one running, making a circle.

qa.q: What might Madhuri be feeling when she asks again, louder?
qa.a: She may feel anxious and shut out, needing reassurance that nothing is wrong between them.

qa.q: What was the turning point on Sunday, and why did it help?
qa.a: Madhuri showed the loop as "us", not one person's fault, which let Jeevan relax and stay to talk.

qa.q: How might Jeevan see the whiteboard drawing?
qa.a: He may feel relieved not to be blamed, which is why he laughs and stays at the table.

grounding: A brother watches a couple's pursue-and-withdraw loop and sees it ease once they treat it as a shared pattern rather than one person's fault.

subtype: Patterns triggered by a partner's style [Observer]
passage:
Diwali weekend: At the family lunch, Chetan watched his cousin Irawati and her husband Deven. Irawati kept asking why Deven was so quiet; the more she asked, the further he retreated, until he was on the terrace with the kids.
Two weeks later: Chetan had them over for dinner and saw it again, only faster. Afterwards Irawati cried in his kitchen. "Why does he always run?" Chetan said carefully, "Maybe you both have a part. You chase when he goes quiet, he goes quiet when you chase. Like a see-saw."
New Year's Eve: At the party, when Deven went quiet, Irawati said lightly, "See-saw moment?" Deven smiled. "Yes. Give me ten minutes, then I'm back." He came back in ten.

qa.q: Where did Deven retreat to at the Diwali lunch?
qa.a: He retreated to the terrace with the kids.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling when she cried in Chetan's kitchen?
qa.a: She felt hurt and frustrated, believing Deven always runs from her.

qa.q: What turning point did Chetan offer, and why did it help?
qa.a: He described the pattern as a see-saw they both take part in, which let them spot it together instead of blaming one person.

qa.q: How might Deven feel when Irawati says "See-saw moment?" lightly?
qa.a: He probably feels understood rather than chased, so he can say what he needs and come back.

grounding: Over several weeks, a cousin watches a pursue-and-withdraw loop and helps the couple see it as a shared pattern, which opens a way out.
